title: Claiborne Williams as teacher and his brother George's fatal illness
summary: He compares Claiborne Williams to Dave Perkins as a teacher of both races, and tells his father's story of Claiborne's travelling brother George, a trombonist who died after a pneumonia while Claiborne nursed him.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yeah. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . And Claiborne, I would say, was like when I came to New Orleans, like Dave Poikin was. He taught both white and colored. Because I remember there was a white student and he had to go to their house and teach them, you see. And he was very known, I mean, as a very good teacher because there were many good musicians that came in colored and white that came to be a good musician that he had actually started. Now he was another one that used to go away with the shows and things. And he had a brother, which my father always told me, that played trombone. My father always put it this way because my father always used to listen to the famous band. I remember his famous band was like Wayne King and Guy Lombardo and this other fellow that played the trombone, Tommy Dawson. He said every time he heard Tommy Dawson, it reminded me of Claiborne's brother, George. Now George, he told me, was what you call an adventure fellow. He always did travel with shows. He never stayed around Donaldsonville so very much. He'd come back when the season would be over and say most of the time he'd come back, he'd be sick. And my father told me this story about George William that the last time he came back there, he was very sick. But it seemed like it must have been a cold, must have had a very bad case of pneumonia. Anyhow, there was some kind of medicine they had. The doctor had to send over to France to get, to rub him with. And he said his own brother, Claiborne William, nobody else didn't want to rub him because he was afraid they would, you know. My father said he was the one that went over there and volunteered to rub him down and put this particular salve on because the doctors there had recommended this was the only thing that was going to do him any good. But he finally died from the stir the way my father told me about it and he was a very close friend to the family of my mother and him. He knew my mother's sisters and brothers and all of them and my grandfather and all of them because if I can recall a block, we didn't live but two half a block from the Claiborne on the same street. But it was going the opposite direction from the railroad which I remember was going back to the graveyard because I have a sister that was her pirate and we used to call him Mr. Tellers for, he was the one that took care of the graveyard back up there. And the family on the other side, they still have a tomb there.
